Let’s dive into Chapter 9: The Illusion of Meritocracy and the Realities of Privilege.
The idea of meritocracy—it’s a story we all know. If you’ve got talent and you work hard, you’ll be rewarded. Anyone can make it to the top, right?
But let’s be honest: for lots of people, the path isn’t so simple. There are roadblocks that have nothing to do with how skilled or determined you are.
Picture this: a young college grad, excited for her first big job. She sends out application after application, giving it her all. But who gets the interviews? More often than not, it’s the folks with connections, the perfect résumé, or just the right background. She works twice as hard, but those doors just don’t open. The system claims it rewards merit, but does it really feel that way?
Here’s something to pay attention to—most of us don’t spot the hidden advantages that tip the scales. Things like family wealth, who you know, or even how you talk and look can swing the odds in your favor. This whole myth of meritocracy? It makes it easy to miss these barriers. And sadly, it’s also easier to blame people who are struggling, as if it’s all their fault.
Sometimes, focusing only on merit can actually excuse inequality. If we believe that every winner truly deserves it, then anyone who doesn’t make it must’ve done something wrong. That mindset chips away at our empathy, making it tougher to create a society where everyone really does get a fair shot.
The reality is, talent is everywhere—but opportunity isn’t. If we want to make things better, we’ve got to look past the surface. We need to ask tough questions about how we define and reward success. It means noticing all the ways privilege shapes outcomes, and then doing the work to level the playing field.
So, here’s the key takeaway: meritocracy is a great ideal, but it’s not how things actually work. If we want a fairer world, we have to admit that luck, privilege, and support all play a part. And most importantly, we need to make choices that give everyone a real chance to succeed.
